Novel Approach: The Hiro Collection.d: A reprint collection gathering six novels that follow Hiro Nakamura: Walls, Part 2; The Trial of the Black Bear; Past Experience; Baby Power; Stolen Fate; and The Trip, Part 1. Nothing in it was new -- it was a way back in for readers who had lost the thread.

The Rogue.d: At a frathouse in Costa Verde, CA , college students Derek and Rick , hoping to join a fraternity , are sent on a scavenger hunt by the pledgemaster . They stop by Costa Verde High School to obtain their first item.

The Last Shangri-La.d: In Goa , Traveler is asked by Hana Gitelman to deliver a message to a man named Drucker in the Kingdom of Bhutan . He enters the country, and easily adapts to his surroundings thanks to his command of languages . Traveling on foot, he soon reaches a village in the mountains.

1x00.d: The cut NBC never aired: longer than the broadcast premiere, differently assembled, and the only episode of the series that was never sold anywhere. It opens on Peter Petrelli standing at the edge of a New York rooftop, falling forward -- and waking in an apartment as Simone Deveaux comes in. It did play to an audience once, in full, at San Diego Comic-Con in July 2006, two months before the premiere -- 72 minutes, with a whole terrorist plot and an evo called Amid Halebi that no broadcast version kept. It was cut from there to the episode-length In His Own Image, and trimmed again into Genesis.

38.vn: Parts 1 and 2 went out together on 19 November 2015 and survive as one video. Part 2 starts about half a minute in.

Making of the Damen Peak Video, Part 1.d: A two-part behind-the-scenes piece on the Damen Peak shorts, posted during the Heroes Reborn campaign and lost when the channel carrying it went down.

Making of the Damen Peak Video, Part 2.d: The second half of the Damen Peak making-of. Like the first, no copy is known to survive.

HeroTruther: 4th of July Fail: Exploding.note: Re-uploaded to YouTube by a viewer -- the only one of the five known to survive.

Claire & the Cat flash animation.d: A short Flash animation of Claire rescuing a cat out of a tree and walking away from the fall, drawn to sell the premise before there was a series. It went up on Tim Sale's own site on 7 June 2006, where the way the site was built meant nothing ever cached it, and briefly onto NBC.com that August -- then came down before the pilot aired.

Heroes Reborn app.d: NBC's companion app for the event series, first mentioned in July 2015. It carried the old show and the new at once: character-by-character routes through all four seasons with the key scenes attached, "speed binge" cuts of every episode, links out to iTunes for the full ones, and the Dark Matters shorts as they went up.

Global News Interactive / The Drucker Fi.d: An in-fiction news documentary on Richard Drucker, run by the news service Global News Interactive in two parts and four clips, which Hana Gitelman posted to her blog on 13 December 2007. It gives him a whole life: born in a forest in 1943, left on a monastery's steps, adopted in Argentina, and set on wiring the world together from a university in Virginia to Bangalore.
Global News Interactive / The Drucker Fi.vn: The nine-minute cut off the season two set, uploaded by a collector.

Takezo Kensei: Sword Saint.vn: All five parts, as the season two set collected them, uploaded by a collector.

Habbo's Interactivity.d: NBC ran a chapter of the story inside Habbo, the teenage virtual hotel. Paintings appeared in the Heroes group showing scenes from campaigns that had not happened yet; then Syn Anders came forward -- an evo who could work on a person's mood by touching them -- asking whoever had painted them to explain how they knew. A quiz handed every player an ability and a sticker to wear, and a quest ran from Primatech's assignment tracker through a barman called Gary in the Dusty Lounge to a room whose password was Odessa. The last stage was to build decoy rooms, so that whoever was hunting Syn would have too many places to look. It ran from 23 January to 9 February 2009, and it was not the first campaign the two had run together.

Heroes Reborn: Enigma (iOS/Android).d: A first-person puzzle game for phones and tablets, out on 8 October 2015 at $4.99, and one of two prequels to the event series: Phosphor built both, under Tim Kring's Imperative Entertainment, and two of the show's own writers scripted them. You play Dahlia, fourteen, trying to get out of the Quarry across thirty-two rooms, using telekinesis and then -- after an injection of the Gemini formula -- the ability to slow time and to shift between 2008 and 2014. Its designer named Portal as the model.

Gemini: Heroes Reborn (PC/PS4/XBOX One).d: The other half of Enigma, and the bigger one: a first-person action game on Xbox One, Steam and PC from 19 January 2016, with the PlayStation 4 version a week later. You play Cassandra Hays, Dahlia's younger sister, twenty years old, with telekinesis and a local kind of time travel that rewinds the room around her to get past what is in it. The two games interlock but stand alone, and both run ahead of the series, in 2008 and 2014.

Season 1 Extras: 50 deleted scenes.d: Cut material from nineteen of the twenty-three episodes. Mostly extensions rather than lost plot -- the exception is Genesis, whose trims belong to the terrorist thread the series dropped. Runs about 49 min on the season one DVD.

Season 1 Extras: Mind Reader game.d: A numerical parlour trick on disc five, dressed up as a test of Matt Parkman's telepathy. On the season one DVD.

Season 2 Extras: 17 deleted scenes.d: Trims from six episodes -- an alternate opening for Nathan, more of Hiro in feudal Japan, more of Monica in New Orleans. Runs about 24 min on the season two set.

Season 2 Extras: Generations alternate e.d: The finale as it was first cut, reusing much of the aired footage but sending the virus somewhere very different. Runs about 18 min on the season two set.

Season 2 Extras: Untold Stories.d: Scenes shot for the twelfth and thirteenth episodes of a season that stopped at eleven. Mostly Elle hunting Sylar. Runs about 12 min on the season two set.

Season 2 Extras: NBC.com featurettes.d: Three web teasers made to look like camera-phone footage: Hotel Corinthian Explosion, Maya y Alejandro Viral Video, and Nathan and Peter Brooklyn Cam. Runs about 4 min on the season two set.

Season 3 Extras: 36 minutes of deleted s.d: Includes the Hard Knox webisodes, cut in among the trims rather than listed as a series of their own. Runs about 36 min on the season three set.

Season 3 Extras: Pinehearst Commercial.d: A mock advertisement for the company's civilian front. Runs about 1 min on the season three set.

Season 4 Extras: 45 minutes of deleted s.d: Trims across the season, spread over all four discs. Runs about 45 min on the season four set.

Heroes Reborn Extras: 17 deleted scenes.d: Trims from nine of the thirteen episodes. Runs about 18 min on the Heroes Reborn set.

Inside Heroes #1: Visual Effects.d: Mark Kolpack, Anthony Ocampo and Ryan Wieber of Stargate Digital drew the line between a special effect, which happens on set, and a visual effect, which happens after the shoot -- then took the Tokyo street where Hiro stops time apart pass by pass: 3D objects built, real camera moves matched to digital ones, green rigging painted out, grain and focus added last so none of it shows.

Inside Heroes #2: The Score.d: Wendy Melvoin, Lisa Coleman and engineer Michael Perfitt on writing a film's worth of music every week. They read the first scripts expecting to go orchestral, then heard Shenkar and built the sound around his voice instead -- one held note that belongs to nothing else. Coleman called the score another character; Perfitt called the schedule a marathon.

Inside Heroes #3: Wardrobe.d: Costume designer Debra McGuire dressed the series by palette -- red, white and blue for Texas, sombre greys for New York, black and white for Japan -- and had to build clothes that could also be aged, blood-soaked, or torn open by a bone coming through on cue.

Inside Heroes #4: Stunts.d: Stunt coordinator Ian Quinn on why nearly every episode has stunt work: it is how an ability gets shown rather than described. He tested each one himself first, then let the actors do as much of it as the risk allowed, which he thought was what made it read as real.

Inside Heroes #5: Makeup.d: Lori Madrigal's department, filmed around the fire at the end of Company Man. Prosthetic burns are cast and laid out to dry, a stand-in is made up in three grades of charring for three stages of the scene, and hot gel goes onto Jack Coleman's arm.

Inside Heroes #6: Craft Services.d: John Hinterlong fed more than 150 people across several units at once out of a small kitchen, and kept the standing orders straight: Milo Ventimiglia vegetarian, Hayden Panettiere's French onion soup, Greg Grunberg on protein and no sugar.

Inside Heroes #7: The Artwork.d: Tim Sale on painting everything Isaac Mendez paints. He is colour-blind and not a painter by training, so he worked in greyscale on a computer and let that be turned into the canvas that went on set -- including the train wreck, worked up from a photograph into a prophecy.

Inside Heroes #8: Production Design.d: Ruth Ammon designed to the words in the script and gave each character a look of their own. She walks through Mohinder's apartment motif by motif -- the objects from India, the scars flying glass left in the kitchen -- and, having not been told where the story was going, explains why the sets were built to be changed. She also gave away rather more of season two than she meant to.

Inside Heroes: Heroes Webisode Behind th.d: The ninth Inside Heroes, made a year after the other eight. Tim Kring on why the webisodes existed at all -- to go further into the mythology than an episode had room for, and to let a character live online before crossing into the show -- with Rebeka Montoya and Kiko Ellsworth on Going Postal and on Echo's ability.

Heroes: Countdown to the Premiere.d: NBC's own hour of countdown ahead of the Volume Three premiere. Masi Oka introduces a scene from The Second Coming, and a montage runs back through the story so far and through how far the show had travelled -- the references, the awards, the audiences abroad.

Unmasked: A Heroes Welcome.d: One of two Unmasked programmes Heroes Wiki's episode list leaves out, so there is no summary of it to quote. The BBC broadcast survives on archive.org and plays here; the archive item files it as the ninth of season one.

Unmasked: Heroes Return.d: The other one the wiki's list skips. The archive item files it ahead of Japanese Idol as season two, episode zero -- the programme that opened Unmasked's second run. It plays here.

Season 1 Extras: The Making of Heroes.d: The short official overview: where the idea came from, how the cast was found, the Comic-Con debut that made it a phenomenon before it aired. Runs about 10 min on the season one DVD.

Season 1 Extras: Special Effects.d: The difference between an effect done on set and one done in a computer, worked through on the scene where Hiro stops time in a Tokyo street. Runs about 9 min on the season one DVD.

Season 1 Extras: The Stunts.d: Stunt coordinator Ian Quinn on how the falls and fights were staged, with raw on-set footage of the takes. Runs about 10 min on the season one DVD.

Season 1 Extras: A Profile of Artist Tim.d: The comics artist who painted everything Isaac Mendez paints, on his career and on working colour-blind. Runs about 11 min on the season one DVD.

Season 1 Extras: The Score.d: Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman on writing and recording the series' music. Runs about 9 min on the season one DVD.

Season 1 Extras: Episode Commentaries.d: 13 tracks on the season one DVD, covering the unaired pilot (Tim Kring alone), Godsend, The Fix, Distractions, Run!, Unexpected, Company Man, Parasite, .07%, Five Years Gone, The Hard Part, Landslide and How to Stop an Exploding Man. Cast, directors and writers rotate through each one rather than sitting the whole episode.

Collector's Edition Extras: Cast at the.d: A bonus disc unique to the Collector's Edition: three quarters of an hour of the cast and crew in conversation at the Museum of Television and Radio, sold nowhere else. Runs about 45 min on the Collector's Edition.

Collector's Edition Extras: Four Miniatu.d: Not a feature but four objects in the box: miniature reproductions of Isaac Mendez's prophetic canvases, painted for the series by Tim Sale. On the Collector's Edition.

Season 2 Extras: Heroes Season Two: A Ne.d: A promotional overview of the new season and its new characters, made to be watched before the episodes rather than after. Runs about 15 min on the season two set.

Season 2 Extras: Genetics of a Scene.d: Allan Arkush and Greg Beeman take a few scenes apart and explain what it took to shoot each one. Runs about 23 min on the season two set.

Season 2 Extras: Season Three Sneak Peek.d: Cast and crew promising the next year will be extraordinary, with almost no detail attached. Runs about 9 min on the season two set.

Season 2 Extras: Behind the Alternate En.d: Tim Kring, Jeph Loeb and Jesse Alexander on why the ending changed -- the one place on any of these discs where the writers' strike is discussed directly. Runs about 11 min on the season two set.

Season 2 Extras: Tim Sale Gallery of Scr.d: Close-ups of the paintings Sale made for the series. Runs about 2 min on the season two set.

Season 2 Extras: Episode Commentaries.d: 11 tracks on the season two set, covering all eleven episodes, from Four Months Later... to Powerless. Cast, directors and writers rotate through each one rather than sitting the whole episode.

Season 3 Extras: The Super Powers of Her.d: Stunt coordinator Tim Gilbert on staging the abilities, with before-effects footage of how the shots actually looked on set. Runs about 8 min on the season three set.

Season 3 Extras: Completing the Scene.d: The effects team on turning those plates into finished shots, including the ruined-future sequence. Runs about 8 min on the season three set.

Season 3 Extras: The Prop Box.d: A walk through the show's gold room, where the props worth keeping ended up -- including Isaac's original canvases. Runs about 5 min on the season three set.

Season 3 Extras: Genetics of a Scene.d: Four segments on specific shots: Claire's brain, the deformed test subject's prosthetics, Daphne's speed, and the Matt-and-Danko chase. Runs about 20 min on the season three set.

Season 3 Extras: The Writer's Forum.d: Tim Kring, Adam Armus and Aron Eli Coleite on what they were trying to do with the Villains and Fugitives volumes. Runs about 13 min on the season three set.

Season 3 Extras: Tim Sale Gallery of Scr.d: The season's paintings, including the ones painted onto rock. Runs about 1 min on the season three set.

Season 3 Extras: Episode Commentaries.d: 25 tracks on the season three set, covering all twenty-five episodes of Villains and Fugitives. Cast, directors and writers rotate through each one rather than sitting the whole episode.

Season 4 Extras: Deconstructing Sylar.d: Zachary Quinto, Tim Kring and Adam Armus on the character the series could never quite finish with. Runs about 21 min on the season four set.

Season 4 Extras: Heroes Revolution.d: How the comics, the webisodes and the online campaign were meant to fit around the show. Runs about 11 min on the season four set.

Season 4 Extras: Milo Speaks.d: Milo Ventimiglia on comics, and on the ones he was publishing himself. Runs about 5 min on the season four set.

Season 4 Extras: Genetics of a Scene.d: The longest of these: several sequences taken apart shot by shot, including the car filling with water. Runs about 42 min on the season four set.

Season 4 Extras: Message from Tim Kring.d: Recorded after the cancellation and hidden before the last episode, saying the story was not finished. Runs about 4 min on the season four set.

Season 4 Extras: Sullivan Brothers Desig.d: Design work for the carnival. Runs about 2 min on the season four set.

Season 4 Extras: Episode Commentaries.d: 4 tracks on the season four set, covering Once Upon a Time in Texas, Shadowboxing, The Fifth Stage and Brave New World. Cast, directors and writers rotate through each one rather than sitting the whole episode.

Heroes Reborn Extras: Reliving the Legac.d: Tim Kring and the cast, old and new, on returning to the story five years after it ended. Runs about 11 min on the Heroes Reborn set.

Are You A Hero?.d: An abilities quiz NBC.com put up on 8 January 2007, in the middle of season one's winter break. It worked the way the show's own mythology did -- do you believe you have unique or special abilities, is your intelligence logic or instinct, are instincts unconscious thoughts or unconscious feelings -- and branched down to one of ten powers, then handed back the HTML for a banner saying which character you came out as, to paste onto your own page.

Heroeswiki.com.d: A non-profit fan wiki started on 10 October 2006, a week after the pilot aired, to hold everything about the series in one place. It outlived NBC's own site, and it is still the fullest record of the show that exists -- most of the blurbs on this page come from it.

Topps Heroes Series 1 Trading Card Set.d: Topps' first Heroes set: 90 base cards, seven to a pack, 24 packs to a hobby box, eight boxes to a case. Seeded through it were ten autographs on sticker signatures, five costume-swatch cards, ten foils, retail-only motion lenticulars, and sketch cards drawn by forty-five different artists -- Tim Sale, who painted for the show, among them.

Topps Heroes Series 2 Trading Card Set.d: The second set, drawn from season two: another 90 base cards, seven to a pack and 24 packs to a box, but ten boxes to a case. The inserts were the point of it -- fourteen autographs, five dual autographs, ten costume cards, five dual costumes, four autographed costumes, sketches and foils -- and every box was guaranteed one of them.

Heroes: Some People Are Born to Be Extra.d: A 566-page TV Guide book credited to Tim Kring, out a few months before Heroes Reborn: a summary of all 78 episodes of the original run, about seven pages and a set of screen grabs each.

Heroes Character Profiles.d: Opened on NBC.com the same day as Inside Heroes, and meant to do the opposite job: instead of showing how the show was made, retrace one character's season from the beginning. Peter Petrelli's went up first, on 21 May 2007, followed through the summer by Claire Bennet, Hiro Nakamura, Nathan Petrelli, Niki/Jessica Sanders, Matt Parkman and Mohinder Suresh among others.

Heroes World Tour.d: A promotional tour through several cities between 27 August and 1 September 2007, timed to land on the season one DVD and carry into the season two premiere.

Heroes All Access official fan club webs.d: NBC's paid fan club, live from 9 April 2009 and reached through a myNBC account: wallpapers and downloads, members-only merchandise, discounted tickets to Heroes events, and a news blog written by the cast and crew. Joining brought a kit six to eight weeks later -- welcome letter, certificate, card, T-shirt, sketchbook and patch, with a cap and a backpack for VIPs.

Super Bowl XLIII commercials.d: Three spots during NBC's Super Bowl broadcast on 1 February 2009. The minute-long one, "Heroes of the Gridiron", puts the cast on a football field against NFL legends: Nathan goes long, Claire flips over a defender to catch it, Hiro freezes time and walks the ball in, and John Elway turns out to be one of them. There was also a crossover music video with Chuck and Medium lip-syncing "Feelin' Alright?", and a straight promo for the Fugitives premiere the next night.

Heroes: The Video Game announced.d: NBC gave Ubisoft the licence at Comic-Con on 26 July 2007: a third-person action game across the whole ensemble rather than one character, for PS3, Xbox 360, Wii and PC. Jesse Alexander said they had been writing towards it from day one -- "All along we've been writing some of our stories in ways they can tie into the eventual video game" -- and it was meant to run alongside season three. Ubisoft was busy with Lost: Via Domus, so High Voltage Software took it on, quietly, and rebuilt the premise around a new redheaded evo of their own who would move through season one's story while dealing with her own. Prototyping ran on the Xbox 360 for under a month before High Voltage realised the company could not carry every platform at once and walked away; the assets went back to Ubisoft, who held the licence in case the ratings recovered. They did not. Ubisoft dropped it around October 2008 and said so that November. All that exists is concept art -- the woman on the card was never even named.

Heroes Reborn teaser in 2014 Winter Olym.d: No press release first: NBC simply ran a teaser during its Olympic coverage on 22 February 2014 -- the logo, the word Reborn, and "Coming 2015" -- and let the audience work it out. The trades caught up the same evening with the rest of it: thirteen episodes ordered, Tim Kring back, and a web series to run ahead of the show.
Heroes Reborn teaser in 2014 Winter Olym.vn: A viewer's off-air recording, uploaded the same night.

Heroes: Origins announced.d: NBC put it on the fall schedule at its upfront in New York on 14 May 2007: six standalone hours, one new evolved human introduced in each, written and produced by a second staff working under Tim Kring at the same time as the parent show, and dropped into the Monday slot whenever Heroes went on hiatus -- twenty-four hours of Heroes and six of Origins, thirty weeks of the franchise instead of twenty-two. Kevin Reilly presented it as the answer to what he called the network's bulk-up challenge, and said the idea had been Kring's. The hook was the vote: once all six had aired, the audience would choose which of the six new characters joined Heroes proper the following season. The names came in over the summer -- Kevin Smith at Comic-Con on 28 July to write and direct the first, then Eli Roth, Michael Dougherty, Jeph Loeb, and John August, whose hour was called Rehab.

Heroes: Origins cancelled.d: Shelved on 31 October 2007, five days before the Writers Guild went out. The Hollywood Reporter called it a false start: NBC would not spend on six hours it might not be able to finish shooting, and rather than delay them it took the whole thing off the schedule. John August, who was to write and direct Rehab -- his was about people who are not good with their powers, and people who are simply not good -- wrote the same day that "the plug got pulled on the six Heroes: Origins episodes". The network never came back to it; asked about the 2008-09 season it said it was better to keep the Heroes mothership as strong as possible. Not one frame was shot, and none of the six characters was ever named.

Heroes: Eclipsed announced.d: Deadline broke it on 10 April 2024, two days after the eclipse that crossed North America: a third Heroes, written and executive produced by Tim Kring with his manager Jordan Cerf, set years after the original run, with a new generation of evos waking to their powers and familiar villains and new ones trying again to put the lid back on. It was a pitch, not an order -- taken to NBC and to the streamers, and bought by none of them. It has been quiet ever since. In July 2026 TVLine's Matt Webb Mitovich reported that Eclipsed is "not active now", which is not quite dead and is not development either. Eighteen years after the pilot, the newest thing in this timeline is still an announcement.
